title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125. An exploratory paired bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. We reconcile the confirmatory McNemar decision and the exploratory bootstrap interval, document verifier scope and blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting, and supply concise per‑pair repair diagnostics with artifact pointers and hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort but risks outages when generated CLI sequences or transient states violate workflow or availability constraints. LLMs are promising translators, yet hallucination and factual errors remain reliability bottlenecks for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. Our preregistered experiment asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI with a small‑discordant‑count caveat; and (4) execution accounting and explicit per‑pair repaired diagnostics with artifact citations.
sections.related_work: Three literatures motivate GVR for NetOps reliability. First, surveys and system papers document active deployment interest in LLMs for intent translation, AIOps, and multi‑agent network management while highlighting hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers [doi:10.1145/3718958.3750537; https://openalex.org/W4411735779; doi:10.1002/nem.2313]. Second, methodological work calls for tool‑augmented evaluation blueprints and end‑to‑end trials that pair generators with deterministic validators and preregistration to avoid post‑hoc analysis choices [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Third, deterministic configuration verifiers and scalable verification systems provide practical oracles for many syntactic and workflow properties, but their modeling limits (vendor semantics, timing/convergence) constrain external validity [https://openalex.org/W4413757123]. Our study situates itself at the intersection: a preregistered paired trial that couples a single LLM generator with a deterministic verifier and a bounded repair policy to measure verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). Primary estimand: paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 intents stratified over 10 synthetic topology profiles. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) was predeclared as descriptive. Generation and orchestration: each intent produced a single shared_initial_generation candidate by gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate via deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and invoked at most one constrained repair prompt when verification failed (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Provider‑call accounting in the execution manifest records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 with stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4 (deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 48bafa8c94272b409a7329e4946995f633a5de7789e5a96fdcef72d3bb127ffe). Deterministic verifier semantics: the verifier performs normalization/parsing, required‑sequence/workflow checks, availability/group constraints, paired‑field/dependency enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields failure; the verifier emits per‑episode verifier_trace JSON objects archived under execution/scoring/ and summarized in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02). Repair policy: a single automated repair prompt includes the original intent abstraction and the verifier violation codes and short descriptions; a repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid=true.
sections.results: Execution and primary counts: completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece): n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; all four repair attempts resulted in verifier passes and correspond to the four discordant pairs. Model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repairs); mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008. The preregistered exact conditional McNemar (conditioning on n = n10 + n01 = 4) computes the two‑sided p as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ n10; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. The exploratory paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 261ec80ea9343fccbcd0a62294f5382773770fd59d387dc9d749de50ca909b3e).
sections.discussion: Inference reconciliation and practical meaning: The GVR controller repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted. Under the preregistered decision rule (exact conditional McNemar) the difference is not confirmatory (p = 0.125). The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but should be interpreted cautiously: the bootstrap resamples pairs without fixing margins and small discordant counts reduce frequentist coverage for percentile intervals; the bootstrap was predeclared exploratory. We therefore report both perspectives and follow the preregistered McNemar decision for primary claims. Verifier coverage and blind spots: the deterministic verifier enforces canonical parsing, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency rules, and exact final‑state matching. These checks are sufficient to detect a broad class of syntactic and workflow errors in our intent grammar and flagged the four repaired episodes; however, the verifier does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing/convergence, session errors, or hardware limits—hence verifier pass is necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient for production safety. Operational cost: observed repair rate = 4/500 (0.8%) and provider accounting records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4). This suggests that a low‑latency verifier plus a bounded repair loop can materially reduce verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at modest model‑call overhead in a synthetic workload. Threats to validity: preregistration, fixed seeds, and complete accounting strengthen internal validity, but construct validity is limited by the verifier abstraction and synthetic device templates; external validity is limited by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies. Real deployments require multi‑model replication, vendor‑specific parsing, control‑plane simulation, and adversarial testing. Because realized baseline success was near ceiling (0.992), realized statistical power was below preregistered assumptions; this explains the small discordant count and the nonconfirmatory McNemar outcome.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (unexecuted here). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; see Disclosure for critical artifact hashes.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm; H2) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the originally planned multiplicity correction across two confirmatory tests is not applicable to the present execution.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08. The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
